blocks.text: The Messages API is Anthropic's core endpoint for conversational text generation, applying the request and response mechanics covered generically in earlier modules, and playing the same central role Chat Completions plays for OpenAI, covered in the previous module, but with its own distinct request shape and conventions.

This topic covers the endpoint and its required parameters, why the system prompt sits outside the messages array entirely, the messages array's own restricted set of roles, the response's content block structure, stop_reason, token usage, and a direct comparison against Chat Completions.
1. The Messages API as the Core Endpoint

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A Messages API request goes to POST /v1/messages and returns content blocks, a stop_reason, and usage

blocks.text: Every Anthropic model is called through this one endpoint, applying the POST and JSON body mechanics covered in the HTTP Methods and REST APIs topics, concretely to Anthropic's own specific provider surface.
2. Required Parameters

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: model, max_tokens, and messages are all required, with max_tokens having no default at all

blocks.text: A request needs a model identifier, a messages array, and, unlike Chat Completions where it is optional, an explicit max_tokens value. There is no built-in default here, omitting it is a request error, not a fallback to some sensible limit.

code.content:
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain recursion simply."}],
)

blocks.text: 3. The System Parameter Sits Outside Messages

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The system prompt is its own top level parameter, entirely separate from the messages array

blocks.text: The single most distinctive structural difference from Chat Completions is where the system prompt lives. Rather than being the first entry in the messages array with role set to system, it is its own separate, top-level system parameter, covered in depth in the next topic.

code.content:
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a concise technical assistant.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain recursion simply."}],
)

blocks.text: 4. The Messages Array: User and Assistant Only

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The messages array only accepts user and assistant roles, never system

blocks.text: Because the system prompt has its own dedicated parameter, the messages array itself only ever carries user and assistant roles, alternating turns exactly as covered generally in the System Prompts vs User Prompts topic from the Introduction module, just without a system entry mixed in.
5. The Response Shape: Content Blocks

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A response carries an array of content blocks rather than a single plain string

blocks.text: Where Chat Completions returns a plain string as the message content, a Messages API response returns content as an array of typed blocks, most commonly a single block with type set to text, whose text field holds the actual generated string.
6. stop_reason

The response's stop_reason field plays the same role as OpenAI's finish_reason, covered in the Chat Completions topic, indicating whether generation ended naturally, end_turn, hit the max_tokens limit, max_tokens, or stopped for another documented reason, the specific field name and values differ between providers even though the underlying concept is identical.
7. Token Usage

A response's usage field reports input_tokens and output_tokens, the same token cost tracking discipline covered generally in an earlier module, just under Anthropic's own field names rather than OpenAI's prompt_tokens and completion_tokens.
8. Multi-Turn Conversations

A multi-turn conversation appends the model's own prior reply back into the messages array as an assistant-role entry before sending the next user turn, exactly the conversation history pattern already covered generally, the system parameter is simply passed again unchanged on every call rather than being repeated inside the array.
9. Comparing Messages API to Chat Completions

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The two APIs solve the same problem with a genuinely different request and response shape

blocks.text: Worked Example

A developer builds a three-turn conversation: a system parameter set once defining a helpful coding assistant persona, an initial user message asking a question, the model's reply appended back as an assistant message, and a follow-up user message referencing the earlier answer, with the same system parameter passed unchanged on every call.

Reading response.content[0].text on each call extracts the actual reply text, while response.stop_reason confirms each turn ended naturally rather than being cut off by the max_tokens limit set on the request.
Common Mistakes

items: Omitting max_tokens entirely, expecting it to default the way it does with Chat Completions
Trying to place a system role entry inside the messages array instead of using the separate system parameter
Reading response.content directly as if it were a plain string rather than an array of content blocks
Confusing stop_reason values with OpenAI's differently named finish_reason values

blocks.text: Practice

Construct a Messages API request with an explicit system parameter, a max_tokens value, and a two-turn messages array, a user question followed by a manually written assistant reply followed by a new user follow-up. Print the final response's content text, stop_reason, and token usage.
Key Takeaway

The Messages API plays the same central role as Chat Completions but with a genuinely different shape: a required max_tokens, a system prompt living outside the messages array as its own parameter, a messages array restricted to user and assistant roles, and a response whose content arrives as typed blocks rather than a plain string, differences worth knowing precisely before switching between providers.
